newsitem.title: USA: Dow flirts with 6000, Nasdaq sets another record.
newsitem.headline: Dow flirts with 6000, Nasdaq sets another record.

text.p: The Dow industrials cracked the 6000 barrier for the first time in history but ended weaker on profit-taking, while the Nasdaq Composite scored its first record close in four months as technology stocks rallied.

The Dow lost 14 to about 5979 after briefly piercing 6000 twice and setting a record intraday high of 6002.17. The Dow on Friday set its 27th record close this year as a weak September jobs report raised hopes for no Fed tightening soon.
The Nasdaq Composite rose three to about 1250.77, topping the previous all-time high finish of 1249.15, set June 5.
The tech-laden Nasdaq index was aided by Intel, up 2-15/16 to 104-5/8 after touching a fresh 52-week high of 105, and Microsoft, which rose 1-1/8 to 137-1/2.
The S&P 500 pushed further into record ground, up two to about 703, its fifth record close in the past six sessions. Likewise, the NYSE Composite rose fractionally to about 375.

"We're recovering from a little nosebleed after Friday's highs, and some people are taking profits off the table. People seem fairly convinced sometime this week we'll close above 6000," said Ken Ducey, head of trading at BT Brokerage.
On Friday, the Dow surged about 60 points.
"It's a bull market. Relax and enjoy it," he said.

As for Monday, Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter, said, "A couple of the Dow stocks got hurt, but oils are very strong and some tech stocks are doing well. The market is consolidating after a big move Friday."

The bulk of the Dow's losses came from Eastman Kodak, off 3-1/4 to 75-3/8. Kodak Chairman George Fisher said the company may remain embroiled in a dispute over opening the Japanese film market for 18 more months.
Oil components Texaco rose 1-1/8 to 96-3/4, Exxon was unchanged at 87-7/8 and Chevron rose 7/8 to 65-3/8.

Oil stocks were bolstered by news of a planned merger of the U.S. downstream operations of three of the world's largest oil companies -- Texaco, Royal/Dutch Shell Group and Star Enterprise, a joint venture between Texaco and state oil company of Saudi Arabia, Saudi Aramco.
Mobil, which already has a downstream joint venture with British Petroleum, rose two to 118-3/4. Amoco rose 3/4 to 72, and Phillips Petroleum was up 3/4 to 43-3/4.
Analysts said technology stocks were aided by the view that some companies would show double-digit earnings growth even as the overall market slows toward single-digit growth.
Among technology stocks, IBM rose one to 127-7/8, Hewlett-Packard added two to 45-5/8 and Motorola was up one to 49-1/4.
Cheyenne Software climbed 7-5/8 to 30 after Computer Associates, up 2-1/8 to 64-1/2, agreed to buy the company for $1.2 billion in cash.

Among individual stocks, Thomas & Betts lost 1-7/8 to 37-7/8 and Augat climbed 4-3/8 to 25-1/4 after Thomas & Betts agreed to buy the maker of circuit connection products in a stock exchange valued at about $550 million.
Westell Technologies tumbled 12-3/8 to 34.
Alpharma Inc slumped 3-1/8 to 11-3/4 after warnings of an earnings shortfall. Oppenheimer and Cowen cut the stock.

Heartport surged 6-3/4 to 36-1/2 after the U.S. Food and Drug Adminstration cleared the company to market its endovascular cardiopulmonary bypass system. Alex Brown raised the stock to strong buy from buy.
CyberCash Inc rallied seven to 40-1/2 after news it licensed its CyberCoin Internet payment system to Netscape, which rose 1/2 to 42-1/4.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 3.31 to 1250.87, a record.
The S&P 500 index rose 1.91 to 703.37, a record.
(Figures official as of 1645 EDT/2045 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk 212 859-1721
